title: YOUR BODY IS NOT DISPOSABLE JUST BECAUSE YOUR SOUL IS ETERNAL
paragraphs: YOUR BODY IS NOT DISPOSABLE JUST BECAUSE YOUR SOUL IS ETERNAL
You may be preparing your soul for heaven while treating the body God entrusted to you as though it does not matter—and Scripture refuses to let us separate the two so easily.
There is a strange contradiction hiding inside the lives of many sincere Christians.
We pray for healing...
while sometimes refusing stewardship.
We ask God for strength...
while repeatedly ignoring the ordinary things within our responsibility.
We pray, “Lord, use me.”

But sometimes we treat the very body through which we serve, work, worship, embrace our children, help our neighbors, preach the Gospel, care for our families, and carry out our calling as though it were disposable.
And because Christians know that eternal life is real, we can accidentally begin thinking as though the physical life God gave us is spiritually insignificant.
After all...
This body will die.
Christ will raise His people.
Eternity is coming.
So why should this temporary body matter very much?
Because it matters to God.
And perhaps one of the most uncomfortable questions a believer can ask is not simply:
“Do I believe God can heal me?”
But:
“Am I honoring God with the body I keep asking Him to heal?”
That question must be handled carefully.
Very carefully.
Because somewhere reading this is a faithful Christian living with cancer.
Someone has an autoimmune disease.
Someone was born with a disability.
Someone has chronic pain despite years of prayer.
Someone eats carefully, exercises faithfully, attends medical appointments, and still received devastating news.
Someone buried a health-conscious husband.
Someone watched a godly mother die younger than anyone expected.
So hear this before anything else:
Illness is not proof that you failed God.
Health is not proof that you pleased Him.
A long life is not God's guaranteed reward for eating correctly, exercising regularly, sleeping enough, or maintaining the “right” weight.
And Christianity is not a baptized wellness program promising that sufficient discipline will prevent disease.
We live in a fallen creation where even faithful believers suffer, weaken, age, become sick, and eventually die unless Christ returns first.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely greater than a guarantee of physical longevity.
It gives us resurrection.
But resurrection does not make your present body meaningless.
In fact, the Christian hope of resurrection tells us something astonishing:
God does not despise embodied human existence.
Jesus Christ did not save some invisible spiritual fragment of you while dismissing everything physical as worthless.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He walked.
He became tired.
He ate.
He slept.
He touched lepers.
He bled.
He suffered.
He died bodily.
And He rose bodily.
Christianity is not the story of human beings escaping God's mistake called “the body.”
It is the story of the Creator redeeming fallen human beings through the incarnate, crucified, and risen Christ.
Which makes Paul's words to Corinth impossible to shrug off.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
The Greek brings Paul's language into even sharper focus:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν... καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν; ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
The heart of Paul's declaration is devastating to the illusion of Christian self-ownership:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν — ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
Then:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς — ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“You were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
δοξάσατε... τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν — doxasate... ton theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Glorify God in your body.”
We need to be honest about the context.
Paul was not writing a first-century fitness manual.

He was confronting sexual immorality and correcting a disastrous view of the body. Earlier in the passage he declares that “the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13, KJV).
So we should not rip verses 19–20 out of their context and pretend Paul was directly prescribing exercise routines, calorie limits, medical screenings, sleep schedules, or nutritional plans.
He wasn't.
But the theological principle underneath his argument reaches far deeper than our modern categories.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
That changes everything.
Your body is not God.
But neither is it garbage.
It is not worthy of worship.
But neither is it worthy of careless contempt.
You are not commanded to become obsessed with preserving youth.
You are not commanded to chase an impossible physique.
You are not commanded to measure your spiritual worth by a scale, a mirror, a blood test, a diagnosis, a clothing size, or the number of years you live.
But you are called to recognize ownership.
You belong to Christ.
That means Christian stewardship can reach places we sometimes prefer to keep outside discipleship.
What we eat.
How we rest.
How we work.
Whether we repeatedly push ourselves beyond reasonable limits.
Whether we seek appropriate medical help when something is wrong.
Whether we knowingly feed destructive habits.
Whether vanity controls us.
Whether laziness controls us.
Whether anxiety about health has become its own idol.
Whether we neglect our bodies because caring for them feels inconvenient.
And yes...
whether we keep asking God to change circumstances while refusing to examine choices He has actually placed within our responsibility.
Not because disciplined Christians never get sick.
They do.
Not because stewardship guarantees tomorrow.
It doesn't.
Not because every illness can be prevented.
It cannot.
But because obedience does not become meaningless simply because outcomes remain in God's hands.
A farmer cannot command rain.
He still plants.
A parent cannot guarantee what an adult child will become.
She still loves, teaches, corrects, and prays.
A Christian cannot guarantee another heartbeat.
We still steward the life God has entrusted to us.
Maybe that is where this becomes personal.
You have prayed:
“Lord, give me strength.”
But perhaps your body has been whispering exhaustion for months and you keep treating rest like weakness.
You have prayed:
“Lord, help me serve my family.”
But perhaps you have accepted patterns you already know are harming you because changing them feels difficult.
You have prayed:
“Lord, heal me.”
And perhaps there is absolutely nothing you could have done to prevent what happened.
If that is your story, this article is not an accusation.
Christ does not stand over suffering believers with folded arms saying, “You caused this.”
Remember the man born blind.
The disciples wanted an explanation they could neatly attach to personal sin:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus rejected their simplistic conclusion.
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents...” (John 9:2–3, KJV).
The Bible gives us no permission to look at a sick person and automatically diagnose a moral failure.
Job should have cured us of that arrogance a long time ago.
Sometimes suffering arrives without giving us an explanation that fits neatly inside our theology.
Sometimes faithful people hurt.
Sometimes children become sick.
Sometimes people do nearly everything “right” and still die young.
Sometimes the strongest believer in the hospital room is the person lying in the bed.
And sometimes the deepest worship a human body will ever offer God is not running another mile.
It is whispering...
“Jesus is Lord.”
through exhausted lungs.
That matters.
Because bodily stewardship is not bodily worship.
There is another ditch on the opposite side of neglect, and Christians fall into it too.
Health can become an idol.
Fitness can become an idol.
Youth can become an idol.
Food can become an idol.
Appearance can become an idol.
Longevity can become an idol.
The mirror can become an altar.
The gym can become a sanctuary.
Fear of sickness can become a master.
And suddenly someone who began wanting to “honor God” spends more emotional energy trying to preserve the body than preparing the heart to meet Christ.
That is not stewardship either.
The goal is not to make your body immortal.
You can't.
The goal is not to make yourself beautiful enough to feel valuable.
Christ already settled your value somewhere far more terrible and beautiful than a mirror.
At a cross.
“Ye are bought with a price.”
There is the center.
There is the Gospel.
There is the reason Christian stewardship can never merely become self-improvement.
The deepest reason your body matters is not because you can optimize it.
It is because Christ purchased you.
Not with money.
Not with accomplishments.
Not because you finally became disciplined enough to deserve Him.
Scripture tells believers that they were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Think about that.
The hands you criticize.
The face you compare.
The body you sometimes hate.
The aging skin you wish you could reverse.
The scarred body carrying memories nobody knows about.
The disabled body someone once made you feel ashamed of.
The chronically ill body that frustrates you.
The healthy body you have taken for granted.

The exhausted body that carried children, worked night shifts, buried parents, survived trauma, served churches, cleaned houses, drove long roads, held crying people, and somehow got you through nights you thought would break you...
Christ's claim over you is deeper than your feelings about yourself.
You are His.
And that means stewardship is not punishment.
It is worship.
Maybe the change you need does not begin with:
“I hate what I have become.”
Maybe it begins with:
“Jesus, this belongs to You.”
My eyes belong to You.
My hands belong to You.
My sexuality belongs to You.
My appetite belongs to You.
My strength belongs to You.
My limitations belong to You.
My work belongs to You.
My rest belongs to You.
My remaining years belong to You.
Even my weakness belongs to You.
Teach me to glorify You here.
That prayer is different.
Because shame says:
“Fix yourself so God will accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ you have been bought at immeasurable cost. Now live like someone who belongs to Him.”
Grace does not say stewardship is irrelevant.
Grace changes the reason we steward.
We are not trying to earn God's love.
We respond because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never earn.
That is the difference between legalism and worship.
Maybe you have neglected yourself for years.
Maybe food became comfort because nobody knew how badly you were hurting.
Maybe exhaustion became normal because everybody needed something from you.
Maybe you stopped caring after the divorce.
Maybe grief hollowed you out.
Maybe depression made ordinary care feel impossibly heavy.
Maybe trauma changed your relationship with your body.
Maybe you spent years serving everyone except the person staring back from your mirror.
Maybe nobody ever taught you that stewardship could be gentle.
Perhaps repentance for you does not look dramatic tonight.
Perhaps it looks like admitting:
“Lord, I have not handled well what You entrusted to me.”
No excuses.
No self-hatred.
No promises that tomorrow you will become a completely different human being.
Just surrender.
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
And there is grace here.
So much grace.
The Gospel is filled with ruined people discovering that Jesus does not merely expose what sin has done.
He redeems what sin has touched.
Peter failed.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him.
The thief reached the final hours of a wasted life and discovered that grace was still standing beside him on a cross.
That is why your neglected years do not have to become your identity.
You may not be able to reverse every consequence.
You may never recover everything lost.
You cannot bargain your way into another forty years.
But you can place whatever remains into the hands of Christ.
One year.
Twenty years.
Six months.
Tomorrow.
This afternoon.
This breath.
Whatever remains can become worship.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not repainting our failures with religious language.
Not hiding our neglect behind “God is in control” while refusing responsibility.
And not pretending our obedience gives us control over outcomes that belong to God.
It is bringing the whole complicated story to Jesus...
the neglect...
the fear...
the sickness...
the shame...
the habits...
the regrets...
the scars...
the diagnosis...
the years we cannot recover...
and discovering that Christ still knows how to write redemption into pages we thought we had ruined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps today you do not need another extreme resolution.
Maybe you need surrender.
Eat with gratitude.
Move according to your ability.
Rest without treating yourself like a machine.
Receive appropriate medical care without shame.
Listen when your body is signaling that something may be wrong.
Reject sexual immorality because your body belongs to Christ.
Reject vanity because your body is not your god.
Reject despair because weakness does not erase your worth.
Reject judgment toward the sick because you do not know their story.
Reject the fantasy that healthy choices make you sovereign over tomorrow.
And reject the lie that because your soul is eternal, your body is disposable.
Your body will not last forever in its present mortal condition.
But what you do with it can glorify the One who will.
Be honest.

And if God has been teaching you the difference between caring for your body and worshiping it, share your testimony. Someone scrolling silently may desperately need to know that faithful stewardship can begin again without shame.
If this truth can help another believer move from neglect, shame, fear, or idolatry toward Christ-centered stewardship, let your share become an act of service.
Send it to the believer who needs conviction without condemnation.
Send it to the suffering Christian who needs to hear that sickness is not proof God is disappointed in them.
Send it to the person who has confused bodily neglect with spirituality.
And send it to someone who needs to remember that Christianity's ultimate hope is not perfect health now, but Jesus Christ and resurrection life with Him.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to biblical truth.
It is helping sustain content centered on repentance, grace, forgiveness, restoration, Scripture, and Jesus Christ.
And if you are ready to go deeper and support the mission:
But before you leave this page, remember this:
One day you will lay this mortal body down—but until that day, let every breath still entrusted to you become an answer to the blood that purchased you: “Jesus, what remains of me is Yours.”
